subject: python
title: Lists & Tuples
description: Slicing, mutation, the list/tuple difference, and the aliasing trap.

content.title: Definition
content.body: A list is an ordered, mutable sequence. A tuple is the same shape but immutable, which makes it usable as a dict key and safe to hand around without copying.

content.title: Slicing
content.body: A slice always produces a new list. The stop index is excluded, and a negative index counts from the end.

content.title: Watch out
content.body: b = a does not copy a list — both names point at the same object, so appending through one is visible through the other. Use a.copy() or list(a).

exercises.question: What does this print?
exercises.explanation: A slice starts at the first index and stops before the second, so [1:3] gives positions 1 and 2.

exercises.question: Which statement about tuples is true?

answers.text: A tuple is always faster to iterate than a list
A tuple can hold only one type of value
A tuple cannot be modified after creation, so it can be used as a dict key
A tuple is just a list with a different syntax

exercises.explanation: Immutability is the whole difference, and it is what makes a tuple hashable — as long as everything inside it is hashable too.

exercises.question: What does this print?
exercises.explanation: b = a binds a second name to the same list object. Mutating through either name is visible through both.

exercises.question: Which line raises TypeError?

answers.text: Line 4 — a tuple cannot be printed
Line 1 — a tuple needs square brackets
Line 3 — a tuple does not support item assignment

exercises.explanation: Tuples are read-only. Build a new tuple instead: point = (9, point[1]).

exercises.question: Complete the comprehension so it keeps only the even numbers.
exercises.code: evens = [n for n in nums ___ n % 2 == 0]
exercises.explanation: The optional filter in a comprehension is an if clause placed after the for clause.

exercises.question: a.append([1, 2]) adds two elements to a.
exercises.explanation: append adds its argument as a single element, so the list gains one item that happens to be a list. extend adds each element.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: nums.sort() sorts in place and returns ___.
exercises.explanation: sort() mutates and returns None; sorted(nums) leaves the original alone and returns a new list. Chaining off sort() is a classic bug.

exercises.question: Syntax
exercises.back: Binds the first element and collects everything else into a list
exercises.explanation: Star unpacking works anywhere in the pattern: *head, last = items takes the final element instead.

exercises.question: What does this print?
exercises.explanation: Multiplying a list repeats its elements. Careful with nested lists: [[0] * 3] * 2 shares the same inner list twice.
